question: Can a compact representation of an LSTM's parameters preserve enough functional information to emulate the network and predict its task or performance, and when does adaptive black-box probing outperform direct weight encoders?

key_findings.claim: The comparison spans six encoders with different symmetry and information tradeoffs.
key_findings.evidence: Layerwise statistics, flattened weights, a parameter transformer, and an LSTM-adapted DWSNet inspect parameters; fixed and adaptive probes observe only input-output behavior. DWSNet is permutation invariant and universal for regular weight-space functions, while functional probes inherit behavioral invariance but cannot distinguish two implementations of the same function.

key_findings.claim: Adaptive interrogation has an exponential query advantage only for specially constructed finite function families, not in the worst case.
key_findings.evidence: Propositions 3.1-3.3 show that either interrogator can identify n distinct total computable functions within n-1 calls and that some families separate adaptive from fixed queries exponentially. The proof family encodes a decision tree; it does not bound gradient-based training, noisy observations, continuous model populations, or the practical number of learned probes.

key_findings.claim: Emulation provides a shared self-supervised objective, but emulatability is explicitly only a necessary representation criterion.
key_findings.evidence: An encoder maps each target LSTM to a 16-dimensional code; a two-layer LSTM emulator receives that code and minimizes rollout prediction loss across many target networks. The authors note that a low emulation loss can encode superficial commonalities if the model zoo lacks algorithmic diversity.

key_findings.claim: Two released zoos provide repeated snapshots rather than 18,000 independently trained networks.
key_findings.evidence: Each zoo trains 1,000 two-layer, 32-hidden-unit LSTMs and saves nine checkpoints plus 100 rollouts per run. One covers 216 related four-token formal languages; the other rotates tiled sequential MNIST. Tasks are disjoint across train, validation, and OOD partitions, but checkpoints from a run are correlated samples.

key_findings.claim: Functional probes dominate self-supervised emulation, especially on the formal-language zoo.
key_findings.evidence: Across 15 seeds, formal-language validation loss is 0.015 for interactive probing and 0.023 for fixed probing, versus 0.043-0.051 for four mechanistic encoders. On sequential MNIST both probe variants reach about 0.017, versus 0.024 for flattened weights and DWSNet, 0.039 for statistics, and 0.067 for the parameter transformer.

key_findings.claim: The strongest downstream advantage is task identification, while simpler properties do not consistently favor adaptive probing.
key_findings.evidence: On the OOD formal-language task, pretrained adaptive probes outperform the other pretrained and end-to-end encoders. For rotated sequential MNIST, both probe types perform well after pretraining and fixed probing is stronger in the purely supervised regime. DWSNet is generally competitive on accuracy, generalization-gap, and training-step prediction.

key_findings.claim: The reported OOD property task is a labeled adaptation test, not zero-shot model-property prediction.
key_findings.evidence: For downstream predictors, half of the OOD model set is included as labeled training data in both pretrained and supervised conditions. The remaining half tests interpolation across held-out models within those held-out task families, which is useful but weaker than predicting an unseen family without any target labels.

key_findings.claim: The released implementation supports the main encoder families but offers limited reproducibility automation.
key_findings.evidence: The public repository contains dataset builders, model and encoder modules, training configurations, visualization code, and a neuron-permutation diagnostic. Interactive probing is implemented as sequential calls through a functional target network. The README only points to a Zenodo dataset and the repository exposes no test suite, pinned experiment command matrix, or result-reproduction script.

method.core_idea: Represent a trained recurrent network either by symmetry-aware statistics of its weights or by a learned interrogation transcript, and train that representation to let one conditional emulator imitate many target networks.
method.mechanism: Each target LSTM is encoded to 16 dimensions. Mechanistic encoders process parameter tensors directly; fixed probes learn a common input sequence; interactive probes generate each input from earlier target outputs. A conditional LSTM emulator learns rollout predictions from the code, after which frozen codes feed property predictors.
assumptions: All target networks share compatible input, output, recurrent architecture, and initial-state conventions.
Observed rollouts sufficiently identify behavior relevant to downstream properties.
The model zoo contains functional rather than merely superficial diversity.
Emulation pressure does not collapse task information into the emulator alone.
Permutation of hidden units is the main parameter symmetry that must be handled.
Small formal-language and rotated-digit LSTMs are useful proxies for broader sequence models.

techniques.role: Chooses later black-box inputs from earlier target outputs.
Learns a shared diagnostic input sequence for every target network.
Uses reconstruction of target rollouts as a label-free representation objective.
Adapts DWSNet operations to LSTM gate and recurrent-weight symmetries.
Separates task families across train, validation, and held-out partitions.
Tests whether frozen model codes predict task, performance, step, or generalization gap.

evaluations.setting: Formal-language zoo: 1,000 two-layer LSTMs, nine checkpoints each, 216 language tasks, 100 rollouts per checkpoint
evaluations.result: Interactive probing reaches 0.015 with a 0.008-0.022 interval; fixed probing reaches 0.023, while direct-weight encoders range from 0.043 to 0.051.
evaluations.baseline: Layerwise statistics, flattened weights, parameter transformer, DWSNet, and fixed probing

evaluations.setting: Tiled sequential-MNIST zoo with random rotation as task and nine checkpoints for each of 1,000 LSTMs
evaluations.result: Fixed and interactive probes reach about 0.017; the closest mechanistic encoders reach about 0.024.

evaluations.setting: Held-out formal-language families with half used to fit downstream predictors
evaluations.result: Pretrained interactive probing is the strongest exact-task representation and generally the best performance representation.
evaluations.baseline: Other pretrained encoders and end-to-end supervised variants

evaluations.setting: Held-out sequential-MNIST rotation range with half used for predictor fitting
evaluations.metric: Rotation, accuracy, step, and generalization-gap prediction
evaluations.result: Both pretrained probe encoders are strong for rotation; DWSNet is more consistent for simpler scalar and checkpoint properties.
evaluations.baseline: Mechanistic and functional encoder variants with and without emulator pretraining

limitations: Both zoos contain only small, fixed-architecture LSTMs on two synthetic or toy task families.
Nine snapshots from one training run are correlated and should not be counted as independent networks.
The interaction theorem is existential and does not analyze learned continuous probes.
Functional encoders cannot distinguish different algorithms with the same observed function.
The labeled downstream protocol uses half of each OOD set for predictor training.
Interactive probing is reported to be unstable for some seeds and settings.
The emulator objective can preserve superficial zoo variation instead of useful algorithms.
The released code lacks end-to-end reproducibility tests and documented result commands.
failure_modes: Adaptive probes collapse to redundant queries or exploit a narrow rollout artifact.
The emulator carries most task information and ignores a low-quality target code.
Hidden-unit permutations or sign/scaling symmetries break an encoder that handles only one group action.
A probe set identifies training metadata but not the target network's causal algorithm.
A stochastic or partially observable target needs more repeated rollouts than the learned budget supplies.
A new architecture changes input/output conventions and invalidates a supposedly architecture-agnostic probe.
Correlated checkpoints inflate effective sample size and confidence intervals.
reusable_insights: Compare parameter and behavioral representations because each intentionally discards different information.
Make an emulator or simulator predict held-out behavior before claiming a model code is informative.
Use adaptive queries only when the task can reward information gain that fixed probes cannot capture.
Split model zoos by task family and training lineage, not randomly by checkpoints.
Test both correct and incorrect symmetry transformations when validating equivariant weight encoders.
Distinguish zero-shot property inference from target-labeled adaptation.
Measure probe diversity and information gain rather than only downstream accuracy.
open_questions: Can adaptive probing be trained stably with an explicit information-gain or diversity objective?
How many stochastic rollouts are needed to distinguish target models at a stated confidence?
Can one hybrid code retain behavioral invariance while recovering mechanistic differences when needed?
Do conclusions persist when all splits are grouped by training run and no held-out-family labels are used?
How do probe cost and accuracy scale to transformers, state-space models, and heterogeneous architectures?
Can representations predict interventions or failures rather than metadata correlated with training?

competitive_landscape.title: Classifying the classifier: dissecting the weight space of neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Eilertsen et al. release 320,000 feed-forward weight snapshots and predict training properties directly from selected weights. The reviewed work targets recurrent models, functional task identity, behavioral probing, and conditional emulation.

competitive_landscape.title: Equivariant Architectures for Learning in Deep Weight Spaces
competitive_landscape.difference: Navon et al. characterize affine permutation-equivariant operations and function-space approximation for feed-forward weight tensors. The reviewed paper adapts this baseline to LSTM gates but contributes mainly the behavioral alternative and RNN datasets.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Functional Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: NFTs apply attention while preserving hidden-neuron permutation symmetries and perform strongly on MLP/CNN and INR tasks. The reviewed parameter transformer is not permutation invariant; its DWSNet baseline is, while probing avoids parameter order entirely.

competitive_landscape.title: Improved Generalization of Weight Space Networks via Augmentations
competitive_landscape.difference: Shamsian et al. identify neural-view diversity and aligned weight-space MixUp as remedies for overfitting. The reviewed model zoos vary tasks and checkpoints but do not isolate effective sample size or augment functionally equivalent recurrent weights.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Linear Probe Generators for Weight Space Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: ProbeGen finds that ordinary learned probes can resemble random probes and shares a deep linear generator across structured queries, improving accuracy and efficiency. It challenges whether the reviewed fixed probes are well learned, but it does not address recurrent adaptive interrogation.

competitive_landscape.title: What Linear Probes Miss: Multi-View Probing for Weight-Space Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: The later work combines multiple functional views to recover information missed by one probe family. It broadens black-box weight-space learning beyond the reviewed single fixed-versus-adaptive sequence comparison and supplies a current test of probe sufficiency.

novelty_assessment: The paper's credible novelty is the RNN-specific empirical package: two public recurrent model zoos, an LSTM DWSNet adaptation, adaptive and fixed functional encoders, and a common emulation objective. Black-box probing, policy fingerprints, model-zoo meta-classification, hyper-representations, and permutation-aware weight networks were already established. The exponential theorem motivates adaptivity but is not an analysis of the learned method. Later ProbeGen and multi-view probing also show that probe structure and diversity are important omitted baselines.
reviewer_notes: Read all 23 cached pages and visually checked architecture diagrams, Table 2, embedding plots, downstream bars, invariance plots, and appendix diagnostics. Audited the public implementation's encoder, dataset, configuration, and training modules and its sparse README/test support. Checked primary arXiv/OpenReview records for weight-space architectures, augmentation, and later probe generators through 2026-08-23.
